questions.q: Ada is logged in and tries to delete Linus's task. Which question decides whether she may do it?
questions.explain: Authentication proves who is calling: Ada is already proven. Whether she may delete someone else's task is authorization, the topic of the Permissions lesson.
options: Authentication: who is this?
Authorization: may this person do this?
Serialization: how is the task stored?
Validation: is the body well-formed?

questions.q: The lesson ties every token to a server-side session. What does that give you that a plain JWT alone cannot?
questions.explain: A plain JWT lives until it expires; the server cannot take it back. With a session, the server looks it up per request, so deleting the session ends the login immediately.
options: Tokens that the client cannot read
A logout that works at once: deleting the session kills its tokens, even before they expire
No need for a signing secret
No lookups on the server

questions.q: How should the users table store passwords?
questions.explain: A hash is one-way: it cannot be turned back into the password, so a leaked table does not leak passwords. Encryption and base64 can both be reversed. There is never a password column.
options: A password column with the plain text, so users can get it back
The password encrypted with a key from the environment
Only a password_hash column holding the output of hashPassword
The password in base64

questions.q: Why does @zudojs/auth hash passwords with scrypt, which is slow on purpose?
questions.explain: scrypt is slow and needs a lot of memory. One login barely notices, but an attacker trying millions of guesses against stolen hashes is slowed down enormously.
options: To make logins feel more secure to users
An attacker who steals the hashes can then try only a few guesses per second, instead of billions
Because fast hashes cannot be stored in PostgreSQL
So that the hash is shorter

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The string describes itself: format v1, algorithm scrypt and its cost settings. The same password gives a different string each time, because the salt is new and random. A fresh hash uses current settings, so needsRehash is false.
options: v1$scrypt$16384$8$5 false false
v1$scrypt$16384$8$5 true false
v1$scrypt$16384$8$5 false true

questions.q: needsRehash(stored) says true. When can you upgrade the hash?
questions.explain: A hash cannot be turned back into the password, so you can only make a new one when you have the plain password: right after verifyPassword succeeds at login.
options: Any time: run a nightly job that rehashes every stored hash
At the user's next successful login, while you have the plain password they just typed
Never: old hashes must stay as they are
By calling hashPassword(stored) on the old hash

questions.q: Why must the JWT signing secret never be written in your code or committed to git?
questions.explain: The secret is what makes a signature trustworthy. It comes from an environment variable (a .env file that git ignores, or your hosting platform), and the app refuses to start without it.
options: It makes the code longer
Anyone who knows it can create a token that says "I am Ada", or "I am an admin"
git cannot store long strings
The secret changes every day

questions.q: Finish requireSecret(env, name). Throw new Error(`${name} must be set to at least 32 characters`) when the value is missing, empty or shorter than 32 characters. Otherwise return it. Never put the value in the message.
questions.explain: !value catches both a missing variable (undefined) and an empty one (""). The message names the variable, never its value.
questions.expected:
JWT_ACCESS_SECRET ok, 43 characters
JWT_REFRESH_SECRET must be set to at least 32 characters
JWT_OTHER_SECRET must be set to at least 32 characters

questions.explain: The package refuses empty secrets, secrets shorter than 32 bytes, and the same secret used for both kinds of token. Stopping is right: a server with a weak key would hand out tokens anyone can forge.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A JWT is three base64url parts: header, payload, signature. accessTtl is in seconds, so 15 minutes is 900. Anyone can decode the payload: a JWT is signed, not encrypted.

questions.q: Which of these may you put in a JWT's payload?
questions.explain: Anyone who holds the token can read the payload with one line of code. Put only non-secret facts there, never passwords, secrets or private data.
options: The user's password hash, so the server can check it quickly
The user's home address, so the app can show it
The user id and roles, which are not secret
The signing secret, so another service can verify it

questions.q: A JWT's payload is base64url text. Finish readClaims(token): take the middle part, turn base64url into normal base64 (- becomes +, _ becomes /), decode it with atob and parse the JSON. This shows anyone can read a token.
questions.explain: No secret was needed to read the claims. The signature only proves the token was not changed; it hides nothing. Reading claims like this is fine for display, but only a verified token may be trusted.

questions.q: An attacker tries to turn Ada into an admin. What does this print?
questions.explain: Changing the payload breaks the signature. "alg": "none" is refused because the package only accepts HS256, whatever the header says. The refresh token was signed with the other secret, so it fails as an access token.
options:
false Invalid signature
false Unsupported algorithm
false Invalid signature

true undefined
false Unsupported algorithm
false Invalid signature

false Invalid signature
true undefined
false Invalid signature

false Invalid signature
false Unsupported algorithm
true undefined

questions.q: Old JWT libraries were broken by tokens with "alg": "none" in the header. Why is @zudojs/auth safe?
questions.explain: The header is written by whoever made the token, including an attacker. A verifier must never let the token choose how it is checked. Even a correct HS512 signature is refused.
options: It removes the header before checking
It pins the algorithm: it only accepts HS256, whatever the token's header claims
It checks the algorithm against a list the client sends
It asks the user to confirm the token

questions.q: Two services share a secret. What does this print?
questions.explain: A token made for the Task API is not accepted by a service that expects its own audience. Note that verifyAccessToken never throws for a bad token: it returns { valid: false, error }, so you must check valid.
options:
true
{ valid: false, error: 'Invalid audience' }

true
{ valid: true }

true
Error: Invalid audience

questions.q: Which use of verifyAccessToken is correct?
questions.explain: It returns { valid: false, error } instead of throwing, and the result object is always truthy. You must check valid, or every forged token gets through.
options: verifyAccessToken(token, config); return next(); — it throws on a bad token
const r = verifyAccessToken(token, config); if (!r.valid) return 401; use r.payload
try { verifyAccessToken(token, config) } catch { return 401 }
if (verifyAccessToken(token, config)) return next();

questions.q: Why does the lesson use a short-lived access token (15 minutes) and a long-lived refresh token (7 days)?
questions.explain: The token that travels most is the one that expires fastest. Each kind has its own secret, so one cannot be used as the other.
options: To make tokens smaller
The access token goes with every request; if it is stolen, it is useless a few minutes later. The refresh token is only used to get a new pair
Because browsers delete tokens after 15 minutes
So users must type their password every 15 minutes

questions.q: Finish newUser(id, body). Return { id, email, roles } where email is trimmed and lower-cased, and roles is always ["user"], whatever the body contains.
questions.explain: Pick the fields you accept instead of copying the body. Normalizing the email means " Ada@Example.com" finds the same account later. The password never goes into the user object; only its hash is stored.
questions.expected:
{ id: 'u-ada', email: 'ada@example.com', roles: [ 'user' ] }
{ id: 'u-mal', email: 'mallory@example.com', roles: [ 'user' ] }

questions.q: The service's verifyPassword here is a plain comparison, to keep the example fast. What does this print?
questions.explain: A wrong password and an unknown email get the same answer. If they differed, an attacker could find out which emails have accounts. The service even does the same slow hashing work for an unknown user, so the timing does not tell either.
options:
ada@example.com -> 401 Invalid credentials
nobody@example.com -> 401 Invalid credentials

ada@example.com -> 401 Wrong password
nobody@example.com -> 404 User not found

ada@example.com -> 401 Invalid credentials
nobody@example.com -> 404 Invalid credentials

ada@example.com -> 403 Invalid credentials
nobody@example.com -> 401 Invalid credentials

questions.q: Finish loginResult(user, passwordOk) for your own login code. user is null when the email is unknown. Return { status: 200, userId } only when the user exists and the password is right. In every other case return exactly { status: 401, error: "Invalid credentials" }, so the answer never tells which part was wrong.
questions.explain: Unknown email and wrong password share one answer. Messages like "no such user" let an attacker test which emails are registered.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The lesson's findUser trims and lower-cases the email, so " Ada@Example.com" finds Ada. The access token carries the session id in its sid claim, which is how verifyToken checks that the session is still alive.
options: ada@example.com 900 u-ada true
Ada@Example.com 900 u-ada true
ada@example.com 900 u-ada false
ada@example.com 15 ada@example.com true

questions.q: Ada is logged in on a laptop and a phone. What does this print?
questions.explain: logout ends one session (one device); its access token stops working at once, long before it expires. logoutAll ends every session of the user: the "sign out everywhere" button.
options:
laptop: Session is no longer active
phone: valid for u-ada
phone: Session is no longer active

laptop: valid for u-ada
phone: valid for u-ada
phone: valid for u-ada

laptop: Session is no longer active
phone: Session is no longer active
phone: Session is no longer active

laptop: Token expired
phone: valid for u-ada
phone: Token expired

questions.q: A session has an idle timeout of 30 minutes, but no absolute limit. What is the risk?
questions.explain: The idle timeout moves forward every time the session is used; the absolute limit never moves. Always set absoluteSessionTtlSeconds, for example 7 days.
options: Users are logged out too often
A session used once every half hour lives forever, and so does a stolen one
The session store fills up in 30 minutes
There is no risk

questions.q: The service has a revocationStore. An old refresh token is used a second time. What does this print?
questions.explain: Each refresh token works once. When an old one comes back, someone copied it, and the server cannot tell whether the thief or the user refreshed first. So it ends every session of that user, even the honest new token, and the real user logs in again.
options:
new pair: true
replay: Refresh token has already been used
new token: Session is no longer active

new pair: true
replay: Refresh token has already been used
new token still works

new pair: false
new token still works

new pair: true
new token still works

questions.q: The package also exports a standalone refreshAccessToken. Why should you use auth.refresh for users instead?
questions.explain: auth.refresh rotates the refresh token, checks the session and detects replays. Without that, a stolen 7-day refresh token keeps minting access tokens.
options: refreshAccessToken is slower
refreshAccessToken only checks signature and expiry: no rotation, no session, no revocation, so a stolen refresh token works for its whole life
refreshAccessToken needs the password
They do exactly the same thing

questions.q: Finish bearerToken(header). Return the token when the header is a string of the form Bearer <token> (the word Bearer, one space, a non-empty token without spaces). Return null for anything else, including undefined. Never throw.
questions.explain: Check the type first, then match the whole header with ^ and $. Returning null lets the middleware answer 401 without a try/catch.

questions.q: In requireUser, a token can be missing, malformed, expired, or from a logged-out session. What should the client get in each case?
questions.explain: Every failure gets the same answer, so the client learns nothing about why. The details can go to your logs.
options: A different message for each case, to help the developer
The same short answer, 401 Login required
403 for expired tokens and 401 for the rest
500, so the attacker learns nothing

questions.q: After requireUser verifies the token, where does the payload go, and why?
questions.explain: context.state belongs to one request, so two requests never see each other's user. A global would mix users up under load.
options: Into a global variable currentUser, shared by all requests
Into context.state, the per-request storage; from then on "who is calling" is a fact the server checked
Back into the request body, so the handler can read it
Into a cookie

questions.q: Ada sends POST /tasks with { "title": "Buy milk", "ownerId": "u-linus" }. Who should own the new task?
questions.explain: Anything the client says about who they are is ignored. The schema only keeps title, and the owner is taken from the token the server verified.
options: Linus, because the body says so
Ada: ownerId comes from the verified token (currentUser(ctx).sub), never from the body
Nobody: the request should fail with 500
Both of them

questions.q: Where does the logout route get the session id to end?
questions.explain: If the session id came from the body, a caller could end someone else's session. The verified token says which session belongs to this caller.
options: From the request body: { "sessionId": "…" }
From a query parameter
From the verified token: currentUser(ctx).sid
From the first session in the store

questions.q: The login schema limits password to 1024 characters. Why have a maximum at all?
questions.explain: An attacker can send huge bodies to make each login expensive. Checking the length first stops that cheaply.
options: Long passwords are less secure
Hashing is slow on purpose, so a 10 MB "password" would make the server burn CPU; it is rejected before any hashing
PostgreSQL cannot store long passwords
To make brute-force attacks faster

questions.q: A cookie is set with HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax. What does HttpOnly do?
questions.explain: HttpOnly hides the cookie from page JavaScript. Secure sends it only over HTTPS, and SameSite=Lax stops other sites' form posts from carrying it.
options: The cookie is only sent over HTTP, not HTTPS
JavaScript in the page cannot read the cookie, so an injected script cannot steal the token
The cookie is deleted when the tab closes
Other sites cannot send it with their forms

questions.explain: parseCookies returns an object with no prototype, so a cookie named constructor or __proto__ cannot confuse your code: there is nothing inherited to collide with.

questions.q: The service locks an account after 3 wrong passwords. What does this print?
questions.explain: After 3 failures the account is locked: 423 Locked, with a wait of 900 seconds. Even the right password is refused during the lockout, or the attacker would simply keep guessing. ADA@example.com is counted as the same identifier.

questions.q: Account lockout is on. Why do you also need a rate limit per IP address on /auth/login?
questions.explain: Lockout counts per account; a rate limit counts per client. Trying 123456 against every email never locks one account, but the rate limit answers 429 after a few requests.
options: You don't: the lockout already stops all guessing
A lockout does not stop an attacker who tries one password against thousands of different emails
Rate limits make logins faster
The lockout only works over HTTPS

questions.q: You run two copies of the server, each with memory stores for lockouts and rate limits. What is the problem?
questions.explain: Memory stores live inside one process. With several servers, implement the same small store interfaces on a database or Redis that all copies share.
options: None, the copies share memory
Each copy has its own counters, so an attacker gets twice the guesses; real deployments keep them in a shared store such as Redis
Users are locked out twice as fast
Logins stop working

questions.q: Build a tiny lockout. Finish createLockout(max). It returns attempt(email, passwordOk), which answers "ok", "invalid" or "locked". Emails are counted after trimming and lower-casing. After max failures in a row, every attempt is "locked", even with the right password. A success before that resets the count.
questions.explain: Check the lock before looking at the password, so the right password does not help during a lockout. Normalizing the email stops " ADA@…" from getting a fresh budget.
questions.expected:
invalid ok
invalid invalid invalid
locked ok

questions.q: In a POST /auth/password route, which step order is right?
questions.explain: The user id comes from the verified token, never the body. Check the current password (same generic 401 if wrong), store the new hash, then end every session so anyone with the old password is thrown out.
options: Take the user id from the body, store the new hash, done
requireUser → validate the body → verifyPassword on the current password → store hashPassword(newPassword) → auth.logoutAll(userId)
Store the new hash first, then check the current password
logoutAll first, then change the password without checking the current one

questions.q: Finish the two task handlers. listTasks(user) returns only the tasks whose ownerId is user.sub. createTask(user, body) adds a task with the next id, the trimmed body.title, and ownerId taken from user.sub, ignoring any ownerId in the body. user is the verified token payload.
questions.explain: Ownership comes from the verified token (user.sub), never from the body. Filtering by owner means each user sees only their own tasks, and Ada's attempt to give her task to Linus is ignored.
